overview: Two papers this week bear on how language handles noise: [a review arguing that noisy-channel inference](#p0) explains both the robustness and the occasional breakdown of comprehension, and [experiments on referring expressions](#p3) in which listeners sometimes reinterpreted unambiguous zero anaphors as ambiguous pronouns when the event made that reading more plausible, especially under noise. The same experiments found speakers using more explicit forms for surprising events, which supports audience design. A second thread concerns what is domain-general versus domain-specific in learning and development. [A proposal for replacing core knowledge accounts](#p2) explains infant expectation-violation effects through attentional biases and perceptual prediction error, while [work on toddlers' modal reasoning](#p1) found much stronger performance when uncertainty concerned an object's kind rather than its location. [Three experiments on auditory and visual categories](#p5) found no sign of abstract representations shared across modalities, even with explicit instructions to draw analogies. Among the more surprising results, [studies of task switching](#p4) found smaller switch costs when people chose their own task, driven by faster switch-trial responses, and [a scanpath analysis of Hebrew word reading](#p7) found that longer words prompted more serial processing whether or not they were familiar. Finally, [two preregistered experiments on judgments of learning](#p6) found a memory cost for unrelated pairs without reliable changes in restudy decisions, which weakens the changed-goal explanation.

papers.title: An Integrated Account of Language Comprehension and Processing as Noisy-Channel Inference
papers.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin, Moshe Poliak, Peng Qian et al.
papers.summary: The authors make the case that the Noisy Channel theory is the best single explanation for why language comprehension is both so robust and so prone to occasional breakdown. The theory combines probabilistic inference with cognitive limits like memory, and they review the evidence for it across many levels of language. They also point out predictions that are distinctive to the theory, say it explains some long-standing puzzles, and finish with open questions.
papers.abstract: Human language comprehension is remarkably robust---we are good at grasping what speakers and writers intend and can even understand them when their productions are not perfectly well-formed. But it is also susceptible to breakdown: we sometimes don’t reach any possible interpretation of the linguistic input and even arrive at interpretations which are incompatible with the literal meaning. We argue that the most promising overall theory of both robustness and breakdown in language comprehension and processing is the Noisy Channel theory, which integrates the roles of probabilistic inference and cognitive (e.g., memory) constraints in language understanding and provides a unified account across many levels of language representation. We articulate the key components and commitments of this theory and review the substantial body of evidence which is consistent with its predictions. We further identify distinctive novel predictions of the Noisy Channel theory and show that it often provides a straightforward explanation for long-standing puzzles. We conclude by reviewing open questions and future directions for the theory.

papers.title: Successful modal reasoning depends on WHAT went WHERE
papers.authors: Peter Mazalik, Justin Halberda
papers.summary: Toddlers do better on some modal reasoning tasks (thinking about what's necessary, possible, or impossible) than others, and this work suggests the reason is WHAT versus WHERE. In matched tasks, toddlers reasoned much better when the uncertainty was about an object's kind than about its location. Preschoolers showed the same asymmetry when understanding words like "can" and "have to," so modal reasoning may emerge earlier than assumed.
papers.abstract: Modal reasoning requires quantifying over possibilities (e.g., categorizing events as necessary, possible, and impossible). This suite of abilities matures during the preschool years, but toddlers perform better in some modal reasoning tasks than others. We propose that these mixed findings reflect a cognitive distinction: toddlers perform worse when reasoning about ambiguous locations of objects (WHERE) than when reasoning about ambiguous kinds of objects (WHAT). In Experiments 1 and 2, we directly compared these forms of ambiguity using matched tasks. Consistent with the hypothesis, toddlers performed substantially better when reasoning about ambiguous kinds than ambiguous locations. Experiment 3 revealed a similar asymmetry in language comprehension, with preschool children showing better comprehension of modal terms such as "can" and "have to" in a What-based task than in a Where-based task. Thus, modal reasoning emerges earlier than previously suggested, and diversity in results reflects differences in how kind and location information are represented and processed.

papers.title: Selection-for-prediction: rethinking early cognitive development
papers.authors: Stella F. Lourenco
papers.summary: Here the proposal is an alternative to core knowledge theories, which hold that infants start with innate, concept-like representations of objects, number, and agents. Instead, infant behavior might come from domain-general attentional biases favoring things like continuity, contact, and synchrony, working with perceptual mechanisms that make predictions. On this view, violation-of-expectation effects come from perceptual prediction error rather than conceptual contradiction, and the framework is meant to explain both early successes and systematic failures.
papers.abstract: For decades, core knowledge accounts have proposed that early cognition is organized by innate, domain-specific conceptual or concept-like representations of objects, physical events, number, and agents. I propose a different starting point: infants' behaviors may arise from domain-general attentional priors-evolutionarily shaped selection biases-interacting with perceptual mechanisms that organize information and support perceptual prediction, rather than from abstract, postperceptual representations. Attentional priors favor ecologically consequential information, including continuity, contact, and synchrony. When such information is disrupted, perceptual prediction error-rather than conceptual contradiction-may produce violation-of-expectation effects. Grounded in constraints on visual input and neural processing, this framework accounts for early successes and systematic failures, suggesting that development begins with perceptual-attentional mechanisms that shape selection, organization, prediction, and learning.

papers.title: Event predictability modulates production and comprehension of referring expressions
papers.authors: Ivan Rygaev, Vera Demberg, Martin V. Butz et al.
papers.summary: When people describe events, how surprising the event is changes how they refer back to a character. In production experiments, speakers used more explicit forms like full noun phrases, and fewer zero anaphors, for surprising events, which fits with them anticipating listener confusion. In listening experiments with added noise, people sometimes interpreted unambiguous zero anaphors as ambiguous pronouns when that gave a more plausible event, especially in noisy conditions. The match between speaking and listening supports audience-design accounts and extends noisy-channel ideas to anaphora.
papers.abstract: When speakers choose how to refer to a previously mentioned character in the presence of several potential antecedents, they experience multiple competing pressures. Predictability is an important factor in this process, and its role in shaping speakers’ choices has been the topic of ongoing debate. Here, we examine how event predictability, viewed as a specific form of information predictability, shapes both the production and interpretation of anaphoric references. In Experiments 1a and 1b (free production), participants described events involving interacting characters. They used overt forms of reference, such as definite noun phrases, more often when describing surprising events compared to familiar ones. Speakers further produced fewer phonologically non-overt forms, such as zero anaphors, when events were surprising. This pattern is consistent with sensitivity to possible listener misinterpretation of non-overt forms despite them being grammatically unambiguous. In Experiments 2a and 2b (speech perception), listeners heard descriptions of the same kinds of events under varying levels of auditory noise. Listeners were more likely to interpret utterances containing unambiguous zero anaphors as if they contained ambiguous pronouns when this interpretation allowed them to construe a more plausible event, particularly under noisy conditions. Taken together, the results show that event-level expectations shape both referential production and interpretation: speakers favor more overt forms of reference for less predictable events, whereas listeners use event plausibility when interpreting potentially degraded input. This convergence between production and comprehension is consistent with audience-design accounts of reference and extends noisy-channel accounts of communication to the domain of anaphoric interpretation.

papers.title: Enhanced cognitive flexibility with self-determined task choice.
papers.authors: Victor Mittelstädt, Hartmut Leuthold, Ian Grant Mackenzie et al.
papers.summary: Most task-switching studies tell people what to do, so this work asked what happens when people pick their own task. Across multiple experiments, switch costs, especially in reaction times, were smaller under free choice than forced choice. The reduction came from faster responses on switch trials, which hints that choosing lets people disengage from the old task or set up the new one more effectively. The authors link this to both better optimization of control and greater motivation.
papers.abstract: Cognitive control-the ability to regulate one's behavior in accordance with internal goals-is fundamental to adaptive behavior. Despite substantial progress in our understanding of different cognitive control functions supporting goal-directed behavior, most studies rely on externally instructed tasks, whereas in real-world contexts, people often have the autonomy to choose which task to perform. Although research suggests that having the opportunity to choose can enhance a variety of psychological processes (e.g., motivation or learning), it remains unclear whether and how cognitive control differs between instructed and voluntarily chosen tasks. The present study addresses this question using a novel paradigm to investigate how one core function of cognitive control-the flexibility to switch between tasks-differs between self-determined (free-choice) and externally determined (forced-choice) tasks. We reasoned that self-determined task choice may enable individuals to optimize control more effectively (e.g., by switching when control demands are relatively low) and/or may motivate individuals to invest more effort in flexibility-related control processes. Consistent with performance optimization and motivational accounts, switch costs in task performance (in particular, reaction times) were reduced under free-choice compared to forced-choice tasks across multiple experiments. This reduction was driven specifically by shorter reaction times on switch trials in free-choice tasks, suggesting that voluntary task choice takes advantage of control processes that promote cognitive flexibility, such as disengaging from a previous task or reconfiguring a new one. Overall, the present study provides new evidence linking self-determined task choice to improvements in higher order cognitive control functions-specifically, cognitive flexibility. papers.title: Learners do not readily form abstract category representations across sensory modalities.
papers.authors: Casey L. Roark
papers.summary: Do we build abstract category knowledge that carries across senses, or does it stay tied to the modality where we learned it? Across three experiments with auditory and visual categories sharing the same rule structure, learners showed no evidence of shared abstract representations. That held even under conditions most favorable to it: conceptually aligned information, the same task, and explicit instructions to draw analogies across modalities. The results suggest category knowledge from perceptual learning is modality-specific.
papers.abstract: A long-standing debate in cognitive science centers around whether our internal representations of the external world are abstract and amodal or whether they are grounded by sensory modality. Perceptual category learning presents a unique test bed of this debate as categories exist within all sensory modalities, but there is mixed evidence about whether people form abstract representations that can be analogized across modalities. In the present study, we examine whether learners form such abstract representations of auditory and visual categories that share the same rule-based structure. Across three experiments, we examine whether learners spontaneously or explicitly form abstract representations across sensory modalities. Overall, we found no evidence of shared abstract representations even in the conditions that would theoretically most strongly encourage it-when information across modalities was conceptually aligned (rather than misaligned), when information across modalities was encountered within the same task (rather than separate tasks), and when participants were explicitly instructed to analogize across modalities (rather than doing so spontaneously). These results suggest that even when abstract representation across auditory and visual modalities is encouraged, the knowledge formed during perceptual category learning is modality-specific. These results highlight the importance of considering the role of modality in category learning and cognition more broadly. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Are restudy decisions reactively altered by judgments of learning? Insights from related and unrelated word pairs
papers.authors: Franziska Ingendahl, Monika Undorf
papers.summary: Making judgments of learning (predicting your own future memory) can help memory for related word pairs and hurt it for unrelated ones. This team tested whether that happens because the judgments change what people choose to restudy. In two preregistered experiments, unrelated pairs showed a memory cost from making JOLs, but restudy decisions didn't reliably differ with or without them. That casts doubt on the changed-goal explanation for the negative effects.
papers.abstract: Recent research shows that predicting one’s own future memory during learning (immediate judgments of learning, JOLs) can enhance memory for related word pairs and reduce memory for unrelated word pairs. It is an open question, however, whether reactive effects of immediate JOLs on memory performance are related to changes in people’s study behavior. The present study addresses this gap by examining whether the requirement to provide JOLs alters restudy decisions. In two preregistered experiments (Experiment 1a: N = 140, Experiment 1b: N = 202), participants provided JOLs or did not provide JOLs during the study of related and unrelated word pairs, made restudy decisions for all studied word pairs, and completed a cued-recall test. Results revealed no reactivity for related word pairs but negative reactivity for unrelated word pairs. Importantly, restudy decisions for related and unrelated word pairs did not differ reliably depending on the requirement to provide JOLs. Overall, the present findings indicate that immediate JOLs may not have reactive effects on metacognitive control decisions and imply that changes in restudy decisions assessed during learning may not underlie negative reactivity of immediate JOLs for unrelated word pairs, thus questioning the adequacy of the changed-goal account as an explanation of detrimental effects of JOLs on memory performance.

papers.title: Serial or Parallel? Sublexical Scanpath Analysis of Eye-movement Sequences in Single Word Reading
papers.authors: Hend Lahoud, Adi Shechter, Titus von der Malsburg et al.
papers.summary: To tackle whether we read the letters of a word one at a time or all at once, this study looked at fixation sequences within single words, which it describes as the first use of scanpath analysis this way. Thirty-four Hebrew-speaking adults read aloud three- and five-letter words and pseudowords while their eyes were tracked. Real words looked more parallel and pseudowords more letter-by-letter, as expected. More surprisingly, longer words tended to prompt serial processing whether or not they were familiar.
papers.abstract: Are the letters of a written word processed sequentially or in parallel? Despite an abundance of research on visual word recognition, the evidence in this longstanding debate rests almost entirely on indirect inferences from word-length effects and conventional whole-word eye-movement measures. We sought direct evidence on the serial-parallel question by investigating sublexical gaze-fixation sequences—so-called scanpaths . This study is the first to apply scanpath analysis to fixation sequences within single words. Thirty-four Hebrew-speaking adult university students read aloud three-letter and five-letter real words and pseudowords while their eye movements were tracked. As expected, real words showed more parallel processing, whereas pseudowords displayed more sequential, letter-by-letter scanpaths. Surprisingly, longer words tended to elicit serial processing regardless of word familiarity. Our findings support the applicability of scanpath analysis in visual word recognition and its potential to open up new perspectives on word-recognition processes.

papers.title: Privileged representational axes in biological and artificial neural networks
papers.authors: Meenakshi Khosla, Sudhanshu Srivastava, Alex H. Williams et al.
papers.summary: Many analyses of neural population codes ignore the native tuning axes of neurons, so this work asked whether some axes are privileged. Using new methods, the researchers found that both brains and deep convolutional networks consistently favored certain axes in vision and audition. Networks trained on natural inputs lined up with perceptual cortex in this respect, which made axis-sensitive similarity metrics better at telling competing models of sensory systems apart. The authors also show that privileging certain axes can help task performance, reduce wiring costs, and improve generalization.
papers.abstract: How do neurons code information? Recent work emphasizes the geometry and information content of population codes, using measures that are blind to the native tunings (or 'axes') of neural responses. But might these representational axes matter, with some privileged systematically over others? We developed methods to test for alignment of neural tuning across brains and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Across both vision and audition, both brains and DCNNs consistently favoured certain axes for representing the natural world. Moreover, the representational axes of DCNNs trained on natural inputs were aligned to those in perceptual cortices, such that axis-sensitive model-brain similarity metrics better differentiated competing models of biological sensory systems. We further show that coding schemes that privilege certain axes can facilitate task performance, reduce downstream wiring costs and improve generalization. These results motivate a new framework for understanding neural tuning in biological and artificial networks and its computational benefits.

papers.title: Spatial Memory Guides Attention before Object Recognition: Evidence from Lateralized N1pc Responses
papers.authors: Chengyu Fan, Markus Conci, Hermann J. Müller et al.
papers.summary: Contextual cueing is the speedup in visual search when a target keeps appearing in the same layout. Here, EEG recordings showed an early N1pc (140-160 msec) after a placeholder display that carried only spatial layout, with no object identity, which suggests learned spatial structure guides attention very quickly. After targets were moved, the effect reversed polarity, indicating attention kept going to the learned location. Later components appeared only once the search display came on, so picking out the target needs object information too.
papers.abstract: Visual search is facilitated when targets reappear within invariant distractor layouts (contextual cueing). Although contextual cueing can bias attention within 150 msec, it remains unclear whether this guidance relies on global spatial configuration or requires object identity. We recorded ERPs while participants searched for targets in repeated versus novel arrays. Critically, each trial began with a placeholder display that conveyed only spatial configuration, preceding the search display by 500 msec. Following learning, targets were relocated and swapped their locations with a distractor in the opposite visual field, such that the overall search layouts remained unchanged. ERPs time-locked to placeholder onset revealed an early poster contralateral negativity (N1pc, 140–160 msec) for repeated contexts, despite the absence of target-specific object information. After relocation, this effect reversed polarity, indicating persistent orienting to the learned target location. A second N1pc, followed by N2pc and CDA, emerged only after search onset. These findings show that learned spatial structure rapidly guides attention, whereas effective selection requires additional processing of object information.

papers.title: Higher stakes sharpen intertemporal choices far less than rational inattention predicts
papers.authors: Sweta Kaman
papers.summary: Rational inattention predicts that bigger stakes make people both discount less and choose less noisily, through a single attention mechanism. Testing this on 39 studies from the ITC Database (5,729 participants, 337,672 choices), the magnitude effect on discounting was robust but weaker than the theory implies. Choice precision rose far more slowly with stakes than predicted, and sensitivity per unit of value actually fell, the opposite of what's required. So stakes do change how future rewards are valued, but not through one shared attentional mechanism.
papers.abstract: People discount small rewards more steeply than large ones (the magnitude effect), and their choices are noisy. Rational inattention explains both with one mechanism: if attention to future value is costly and scales with the stakes, larger rewards are represented more precisely, which lowers both the discount rate and choice noise. We tested this account at scale using the open ITC Database: 39 studies (5,729 participants, 337,672 choices) in which reward magnitude varies independently of the reward ratio and delay. For every study we fitted three hierarchical Bayesian models with the original likelihoods: a descriptive model in which the discount rate and choice sensitivity both scale with magnitude, the rational-inattention model in which a single attention parameter determines both, and the rational-inattention model with one free stochasticity slope. The magnitude effect on discounting was robust (pooled slope 0.70, 95% CI [0.59, 0.82]) but smaller than the value of 1 implied by rational inattention. Choice precision rose far more slowly with the stakes than predicted. Freeing the stochasticity slope improved cross-validated fit in all 37 studies compared (total difference in expected log predictive density 13,233, SE 177). Posterior predictive checks showed that rational inattention makes choices sharpen too quickly as stakes grow. Sensitivity per unit of value fell with the stakes, the opposite of the coupling with discounting that the theory requires. Larger stakes change how future rewards are valued, but not through a single attentional mechanism governing both discounting and choice noise.

papers.title: Towards a taxonomy for visual time perception
papers.authors: Pascal Mamassian
papers.summary: Visual time perception covers many phenomena, and this review tries to organize them into four clusters, each tied to a goal of the visual system. The goals are linking events into a continuous flow, anticipating when events will occur, integrating information into a stable percept, and holding on to a perceived present. The authors sort twelve classic phenomena into these clusters, including temporal order, postdiction, and perceived duration, and describe the main methods used for each. The aim is to move toward a taxonomy.
papers.abstract: The investigation of visual time perception has uncovered a large variety of phenomena, but how these phenomena are related to each other is unclear. The ambition of the present review is to propose a principled way to class visual time phenomena into four clusters. We suggest that these four clusters result from four ultimate goals that the visual system is attempting to solve to stay well connected to our dynamic environment. These goals are to link successive events into an apparent continuous flow, to anticipate when forthcoming events will occur, to integrate sensory information to consolidate a sufficiently stable percept at each moment in time, and to hold on a perceived present so that it can be used to label events on a timeline. We then review twelve classic visual time phenomena and assign them to one of the four clusters. These twelve phenomena include four basic ones: temporal segmentation, temporal order, temporal integration, and subjective simultaneity. More complex phenomena include temporal continuity, the passage of time, perceived duration, anticipation, backward masking, postdiction, specious present, and perceived nowness. For each of the twelve phenomena, we also present the main methodologies that have been used to investigate them. Ultimately, identifying similarities and differences between visual time phenomena will advance our efforts to create a taxonomy of these phenomena.

papers.title: Psycholinguistic norm estimation depends on construct and procedure: LLM ratings, prototype projection, and embedding regression
papers.authors: Jason Timm
papers.summary: Researchers compared several ways of estimating psycholinguistic norms, including zero-shot ratings from six LLMs, a prototype-based embedding axis, and supervised regression on GloVe and BGE embeddings, across 18 dimensions. Agreement with human ratings varied a lot by construct. BGE ridge regression did best on average (r = .734), the six-LLM mean reached .685, and the LLMs showed very similar profiles across dimensions. Combining the LLM mean with BGE did better still, so the authors conclude these methods aren't interchangeable measurements.
papers.abstract: Psycholinguistic norm estimation can use verbal instructions, labeled prototypes, or continuously rated training examples, but these procedures need not measure a construct identically. We compared zero-shot ratings from six large language models (LLMs), a prototype-defined BGE embedding axis, and supervised GloVe and BGE regression across 18 dimensions and a common 1,636-word holdout. Correspondence with human ratings was strongly construct-dependent. BGE ridge had the highest mean correlation (*r* = .734) and led the individual estimators on 13 dimensions, followed by the six-LLM mean (*r* = .685), GloVe (*r* = .652), and the highest-performing individual LLM, Gemini 3.6 Flash (*r* = .640). The six LLMs nevertheless showed highly concordant dimension profiles (Kendall's *W* = .945). The constrained BGE axis averaged *r* = .624 and had reliably higher correlations than Gemini on six dimensions and lower on ten, showing that the prototype-defined readout was competitive on selected constructs. Raw normalized mean absolute error strongly favored BGE, but out-of-fold linear recalibration narrowed the Gemini–BGE gap from .086 to .009 and eliminated the broad lexical-moderation interactions. Finally, the six-LLM mean and BGE retained complementary variation: their cross-fitted combination averaged *r* = .789, while an outcome-free fixed combination averaged *r* = .774. Automated norm estimates are therefore construct- and procedure-dependent measurements, not interchangeable readouts or entries in a single model ranking.

papers.title: Dynamic learning from good and bad outcomes peaks and persists in adolescence
papers.authors: Katie Oshins, Tejas Savalia, Michelle Sauceda et al.
papers.summary: Participants aged 10-25 did a Pavlovian task with cues predicting gain, loss, or nothing, followed by extinction when outcomes stopped. Conditioned responses to both positive and negative associations peaked and took longest to extinguish in late adolescence, around age 19. Age differences in how readily people attributed changes in contingencies to multiple latent states tracked how persistent those associations were. The authors suggest that learned associations, good or bad, weigh more heavily on adolescent behavior.
papers.abstract: Learning good and bad associations and updating them amidst change facilitates adaptive behavior. Differences in sensitivity to salient, dynamic information from the environment may influence how learning unfolds. Cross-species research suggests that adolescents, relative to younger and older individuals, may exhibit more persistent learned negative and positive associations. However, direct within-person comparisons of valenced learning processes are scarce, and the mechanisms underlying developmental differences in the persistence of learned associations remain unclear. In adults, the persistence of negative associations has been linked to individual differences in how people use experience to infer the structure of their environment. Developmental changes in these same latent-structure inference processes may underpin greater persistence of valenced associations during adolescence. To test this, participants ages 10-25 years completed a Pavlovian learning task in which distinct cues predicted gain, loss, or neither, followed by extinction, during which outcomes ceased. Conditioned responses to both positive and negative associations peaked and took longer to extinguish in late adolescence, near age 19. Negative associations were similarly robustly learned in young adults and weakly persisted in a new extinction context in early adolescence. While a shared latent-structure inference process was observed across valences, age-related differences in the tendency to attribute changes in reinforcement contingencies to multiple latent states mirrored the persistence of valenced associations in adolescence. These findings suggest that while both positive and negative outcomes shape dynamic learning across age, valenced learned associations more strongly influence behavior and cognition during adolescence, as individuals learn to independently navigate a changing world.

papers.title: Visual search with many targets in mind: A successful replication of Drew, Boettcher, and Wolfe (2017)
papers.authors: Joshua R de Leeuw, John H Long, Hana Colley et al.
papers.summary: This is a direct replication of Drew et al. (2017) on hybrid search, where people look for any of many memorized objects. With 38 participants versus the original 14, the results agreed strongly. Fixations on each item got longer as the memory set grew, and refixations were rare, with fewer than half of the items revisited. It was done in a research methods course at Vassar, and the authors briefly discuss the teaching angle.
papers.abstract: We conducted a direct replication of Drew et al. (2017). The experiment examines visualsearch behavior, including eye movements, when participants are looking for one of manymemorized objects. The original experiment found that the search strategy for this kind ofsearch, called hybrid search, involves “one visual search [and] many memory searches.” Ourreplication (N=38) finds strong agreement with the original (N=14) results. As the number ofmemorized objects increases, participants fixate longer on each individual object. Furthermore,refixations are generally rare, with fewer than half of the visual items refixated during search.We conducted this replication as part of the course Research Methods in Cognitive Science atVassar College, and we briefly discuss the pedagogical framing of this work.

papers.title: Do People Use Prior Information to Adopt an Optimal Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff in Experience-Based Risky Decisions?
papers.authors: Amir Hosein Hadian Rasanan, Timothy L Mullett, Neil Stewart et al.
papers.summary: People choosing between two lotteries, with outcomes shown as rapidly changing dot clouds, were tested on whether they adjust how much evidence they collect depending on whether the utility difference between options is known. Theory says a fixed decision threshold is optimal when it's known and a collapsing one (lowering the bar over time) when it isn't. Behavior and cognitive modeling showed no systematic adjustment: most participants looked collapsing-threshold-like in both conditions, so people don't seem to use that initial information optimally. The authors point to epistemic uncertainty, task unfamiliarity, and rising time costs as possible reasons.
papers.abstract: In experience-based risky choice, acquiring and integrating information about the available options is costly in terms of cognitive resources and time. A central question is therefore how decision makers allocate their time to achieve sufficiently high decision quality without incurring excessive time costs. Recent theories formalize this tradeoff and distinguish between two choice environments: When the utility difference between two options is known, and only the identity of the better option has to be identified, evidence accumulation with a fixed decision threshold, that is, a fixed decision quality, is optimal. In contrast, when the utility difference is unknown, a collapsing threshold is optimal, implying that the targeted decision quality is being reduced over time. Here, we investigate whether people adapt their decision thresholds to these different conditions when choosing between two lotteries whose outcomes were presented as rapidly changing dot clouds. Both behavioral and cognitive modeling results indicate that participants did not systematically adjust their decision strategy; across both the known and unknown utility difference conditions, most participants' data were explained better by a collapsing threshold model. Hence, decision makers do not optimally account for initial information about the utility difference. We discuss possible explanations for this, including epistemic uncertainty, task unfamiliarity, and increasing time costs. We conclude that variability in risky choice can be understood as arising, in part, from the tradeoff between the benefits and costs of evidence accumulation, and that cognitive models should incorporate this tradeoff to better characterize rational behavior.

papers.title: Effects of Handgrip Effort on Perceptual Judgments and Metacognitive Performance in Older Adults
papers.authors: Andrew Yi-an Sun, Mohammad Dastgheib, Xiaoping Hu et al.
papers.summary: Older adults did two perceptual same/different tasks, one auditory and one visual, and rated their confidence while squeezing a dynamometer at either a low or high grip force to manipulate arousal. High grip raised perceptual thresholds, meaning it hurt performance, but it improved metacognitive efficiency, apparently through better awareness of errors on the easiest trials. So physical arousal seems to disrupt perception but sharpen how well older adults judge their own accuracy.
papers.abstract: Here we examined how physical-effort induced arousal may have a differential impact on perception and metacognition in older adults. While arousal has been shown to enhance some aspects of perceptual performance in young adults, it can also disrupt metacognitive performance. However, both perceptual and metacognitive functions decline with age, alongside deterioration of neural systems that regulate arousal (e.g., Locus Coeruleus-Norepinephrine; LC-NE). Thus, it is unclear how physical-effort induced arousal influences perceptual performance and metacognitive efficiency in older adults. To test this, we had participants complete two perceptual discrimination tasks (auditory and visual), which involved judging whether two sequential stimuli were the same or different, and subsequently rating their confidence in their same/different response. At the start of each trial, arousal was manipulated by instructing participants to maintain either a low or high hand grip force on a dynamometer. We fit psychometric functions to characterize perceptual performance between grip levels and used the Relative Psychometric Function (RPF) analysis framework to characterize metacognitive ability while controlling for perceptual performance. Across tasks, high grip increased psychometric thresholds, but not psychometric slopes. On the other hand, metacognitive efficiency increased under high grip and was numerically larger in the auditory task, which appeared to be driven by increased error awareness during the easiest stimulus level. Together, these findings suggest that acute arousal can disrupt perceptual performance but enhance metacognitive efficiency in older adults.

papers.title: Limited convergence across established visual statistical learning paradigms: Evidence from a large multi-task study
papers.authors: Eszter Tóth-Fáber, Bence Csaba Farkas, Kocsis Anna Boglárka et al.
papers.summary: Across seven well-known visual statistical learning tasks completed by 192 adults, people showed solid learning and the measures were mostly reliable. Yet correlations between tasks were sparse and weak, while measures from the same task correlated more strongly with each other. Factor analysis gave three factors tied to specific tasks rather than to ideas like online versus offline measures or motor involvement. The takeaway is that these paradigms aren't interchangeable measures of one shared ability, which matters for studies linking statistical learning to language or reading.
papers.abstract: Statistical learning (SL) has been linked to individual differences in language, reading, and other cognitive abilities, yet it remains unclear whether performance across SL paradigms reflects a common underlying capacity. We examined the covariance structure of seven established visual SL paradigms in a large sample of adults (N = 192), spanning different statistical structures, domains, task demands, and online and offline learning measures. Participants showed robust group-level learning in almost all paradigms, and most measures demonstrated adequate to good reliability. Nevertheless, correlations across paradigms were sparse and generally weak, whereas stronger associations emerged among measures derived from the same paradigm. Exploratory factor analysis identified three factors, primarily characterized by measures from the Segmentation, Temporal Visual Statistical Learning, and Alternating Serial Reaction Time tasks, and the results were stable across multiple robustness analyses. This organization did not align with commonly proposed task dimensions, including online versus offline assessment, motor involvement, or statistical structure. These findings indicate that individual differences in behavioral measures of visual SL are largely paradigm-specific, while remaining compatible with the possibility that different paradigms rely on shared underlying learning mechanisms. More broadly, the results challenge the assumption that established visual SL paradigms provide interchangeable measures of a common individual-difference construct and highlight the need to distinguish learning-related from task-specific sources of behavioral variance.

papers.title: Brain activity associated with working memory load and spatial attention during visual change detection
papers.authors: Jenna Laakkonen, Chaoxiong Ye, Lijing Guo et al.
papers.summary: Using fMRI during a visual change detection task, the researchers varied spatial attention cues, whether a change occurred, memory load, and the size of the orientation change. Behavior got worse with higher load and smaller changes, and attention, load, and change each had main effects across many brain areas, but no interactions turned up. About 75% of the areas showed just one main effect, with overlap mostly in parietal, occipital, and a few frontal regions. That pattern points to a fairly segregated architecture for attention and working memory.
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) and attention interact bi-directionally: external cues modulate the selection of stimuli in VWM, while active representations in VWM can guide attention. However, the neural mechanisms underlying VWM, attention, and their interconnection remain poorly understood. In the present study, we investigated functional mechanics of VWM and the role of attention in VWM using a visual change detection task. We recorded brain responses with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine the effects of spatial attention (left vs. right pre-cue), change (present vs. absent), memory load (1, 2 or 4 line orientations while controlling for the number of stimuli), and memory precision demand (15°, 30° or 60° orientation changes). As expected, behavioral performance systematically decreased as the memory load increased or degree of orientation change decreased. Analysis of variance of fMRI activations revealed significant main effects of attention, load, and change across 164 brain areas (determined by Human Connectome Project parcellation), whereas all interaction effects were non-significant. Notably, ca. 75% of these areas exhibited only a single main effect, while two or three main effects converged in 21 parietal, 15 occipital, and 2 frontal areas. Absence of significant interaction effects, combined with multi-feature processing confined to a few fronto-parietal and occipital areas, highlights a largely segregated functional architecture for attention and VWM.

papers.title: Continuous, Discrete, or Both? What Measurement Approaches Reveal About the Nature of Infants’ Word Learning
papers.authors: Melanie López  Pérez, Charlotte Moore, Andrea Sander-Montant et al.
papers.summary: Parents of 8- to 31-month-olds filled out the usual yes/no vocabulary checklist (CDI) and a new six-point certainty version called LAVA. Parents were more uncertain about comprehension than production, and they only marked a word as known on the CDI at high certainty (about 4.7 of 6). In a looking-while-listening task, the binary CDI predicted children's performance as well as or better than LAVA, though LAVA added unique predictive power for words on the cusp of production. The authors suggest the discrete-versus-continuous debate partly reflects how we measure, and they propose a three-phase model of word learning.
papers.abstract: A central debate in early word learning concerns whether it is discrete or continuous. Each view is constrained by measurement format: vocabulary checklists score each word as known or unknown, while looking-time tasks yield a continuous value even for one word on one trial. We investigated whether binary vocabulary measures (parent reports) obscure graded word knowledge, and whether they predict children's continuous looking time. In Study 1, parents of 81 monolingual and bilingual 8- to 31-month-olds learning English, French, and/or Spanish completed a binary vocabulary measure (MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories; CDIs), and a newly-developed continuous adaptation, the Likert Approach to Vocabulary Assessment (LAVA), where parents rated certainty about their child's knowledge of 30 words on a 6-point scale. Parents reported greater uncertainty for comprehension than production, yet set high certainty thresholds before reporting words as "known" on the CDI for both domains (4.7 out of 6). Study 2 tested whether binary or continuous parent reports better predicted children's looking-while-listening performance (n = 71). Binary CDI ratings predicted performance as well as, or better than, continuous LAVA ratings. However, continuous ratings uniquely predicted performance for words on the cusp of production, suggesting sensitivity to emerging knowledge. The tension between discrete and continuous word learning perspectives may stem partly from measurement, with continuous approaches revealing gradations during transitional periods. We thus propose an updated three-phase model of word learning, 1) pre-accumulation: exposure does not contribute to word-meaning associations, 2) active accumulation: learners have emerging word knowledge, 3) post-threshold: word is “learned.”

papers.title: From working memory to long-term memory: The role of focused attention and intentionality
papers.authors: Caro Hautekiet, Klaus Oberauer, Christian Nicolas Leon Olivers
papers.summary: Participants held four real-world images in working memory, with retro-cues directing focused attention to some of them, and were later tested on long-term memory. Some people knew about the memory test in advance, and in one experiment they could earn a bonus for good performance. Attention strongly helped working memory but gave only a small boost to long-term memory, and that boost didn't depend on intentionality. So the idea that wanting to remember is what makes focused attention pay off for durable memory doesn't hold up.
papers.abstract: Although working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM) closely interact, the mechanisms by which WM representations are transferred into durable LTM traces remain unclear. It has been hypothesized that directing focused attention to information in WM strengthens its LTM traces. However, evidence suggests that focused attention offers at best a small benefit for LTM. Here, we propose that attention is necessary but insufficient. Specifically, we hypothesize that when people want to remember information for later, focused attention in WM will benefit LTM more, as it might enable strategic maintenance processes such as elaboration. In three experiments, the first phase consisted of a WM task in which participants memorized four real-world images on each trial. Focused attention was manipulated via retro-cues, and we controlled for testing effects by omitting the WM test on half of the trials. In a second phase, following a brief disruption task, LTM was assessed. Intentionality was manipulated by leaving one group unaware of the LTM test while another group was informed about it before the WM phase (Experiments 1 and 2) or were informed and could earn a financial bonus based on LTM performance (Experiment 3). While attention substantially improved WM performance, it offered only a small benefit for LTM performance; this effect did not interact with intentionality. Thus, these findings confirm that focused attention by itself hardly contributes to creating durable LTM traces, and show that intentionality is most likely not the missing factor.

papers.title: Discourse prominent entities are not cognitively more prominent
papers.authors: Suet-Ying Lam, Shota Momma
papers.summary: Four production experiments tested whether discourse-prominent entities, such as sentence subjects, are more active in memory. The test used pronouns that speakers had to use anyway, and the prediction was that pronouns referring to prominent antecedents would be planned faster. They weren't: subject antecedents gave no speed advantage, and antecedents in a passive 'by' phrase were actually planned faster. Two other possible sources of prominence also showed no benefit. The results suggest prominence in discourse and activation in memory can come apart, and the authors discuss a coherence-based alternative.
papers.abstract: Four production experiments examined whether discourse prominent entities are more highly activated in memory. We developed an explicit information-processing model of how discourse prominence is hypothesized to affect planning speed at each stage of reference production, and tested its central prediction: that a pronoun referring to a more discourse prominent entity is planned faster than a pronoun referring to a less discourse prominent entity, when speakers are compelled to use a pronoun regardless of the discourse prominence of its antecedent due to Principle C. Contrary to this prediction, pronouns with antecedents introduced as subjects were not planned faster than pronouns with antecedents introduced as non-subjects. Instead, pronouns with antecedents introduced as the object of the preposition ‘by’ in passive sentences were planned faster than their subject counterparts. Two other potential sources of non-subject prominence, i.e., the informativity of an optional argument and its status as the source of information, also produced no planning advantage. These findings suggest that discourse prominence and level of activation in memory do not necessarily align, and therefore that discourse prominence should not be defined solely in terms of memory activation. We discuss a coherence-based alternative under which reference to an entity contributes to discourse coherence without necessarily facilitating its retrieval.

papers.title: When Ensembles Beat Items: Conditional Aggregate Dominance in Ensemble Perception
papers.authors: Joss Armstrong
papers.summary: This is a theoretical paper that treats ensemble (group-average) judgments and judgments built up from individual items as two noisy estimates of the same displayed statistic. Under an explicit ordering of their error covariances, the pooled route does at least as well, and it breaks the advantage down into factors like effective sample size, correlated sensory noise, pooling noise, and attentional selection. These predict when the ensemble advantage grows, plateaus, or fades with set size and attention manipulations. A worked numerical example and a proposed matched-report design show how the two routes could be measured and tested.
papers.abstract: Ensemble perception can support accurate group judgements when reports about individual items are poor. We compare pooled and item-mediated routes as noisy estimates of the same displayed statistic. Under an explicit conditional error-covariance ordering, the pooled route has no greater mean-squared error and, for Gaussian mean-shift discrimination, no lower detection power. The contribution decomposes this ordering into effective sample size, finite-population subset error, correlated sensory noise, pooling noise, attentional selection, and comparison or readout noise. These components predict when ensemble advantage improves with set size, plateaus or declines, and survives some attention manipulations but fails under others. Perceptual error is distinguished from variation in the physical mean of sampled displays; poor item memory remains a separate compression hypothesis. A worked numerical example gives predictions with fixed parameters, and a matched report design specifies how to measure both routes and test their ordering in held-out conditions. A display-variance test separates subset from exhaustive pooling with nothing fitted.

papers.title: Measuring Cognitive Noise: Separating Signal Strength from Random Fluctuations in Evidence Accumulation
papers.authors: andreas voss
papers.summary: In the diffusion model, the within-trial noise parameter is normally fixed as an arbitrary scaling constant, which quietly assumes everyone has the same cognitive noise and leaves drift and boundary effects ambiguous. The author proposes two ways to separate signal from noise by adding one assumption each: a Bounded Drift approach that caps maximum drift, and a Random Walk approach where evidence arrives in fixed-size discrete samples. Both were implemented with amortized Bayesian inference in BayesFlow, and simulations showed good recovery of the noise parameters. In a small pilot with five younger and five older adults, the two approaches' noise estimates agreed (r = .74), pointing toward noise as a measurable individual difference.
papers.abstract: The diffusion model decomposes choices and response times into parameters for the speed of information uptake (drift rate), the information required for a decision (boundary separation), decision bias (starting point), and extra-decisional processes (nondecision time). A further parameter, the diffusion coefficient s, scales the random variability of accumulation within a trial. Because the likelihood is invariant to a joint rescaling of drift, boundaries, and s, this parameter is conventionally fixed and treated as a meaningless scaling constant. I argue that this convention implicitly assumes that all persons and conditions share the same amount of cognitive noise, and that it renders drift and boundary effects ambiguous, because only the ratios of signal and boundary to noise are identified. I propose two approaches that separate signal strength and noise by adding one psychologically motivated assumption. The Bounded Drift approach links stimulus information to drift rate through a psychophysical function and fixes the maximum drift at a common value. The Random Walk approach assumes that evidence arrives in discrete samples of constant size at an individual rate, so that sampling determines both drift and noise. Both models were implemented with amortized Bayesian inference in BayesFlow, and simulations show satisfactory recovery and calibration of the noise parameters. In a pilot study with five younger and five older adults, noise estimates converged over both approaches (r = .74). I discuss cognitive noise as a measurable individual difference and outline a validation program.

papers.title: Intact Local Audiovisual Metacognitive Monitoring in Aided Hearing-Impaired Listeners
papers.authors: Perrine Porte, Matan Mazor, Nathan Faivre et al.
papers.summary: Fifteen aided hearing-impaired people and 17 matched listeners did an audiovisual detection task with stimulus intensity adjusted to keep detection at threshold. The hearing-impaired group had lower self-efficacy beliefs about their hearing, but not their vision. Even so, their local metacognition matched controls: confidence for presence versus absence, confidence in multisensory stimuli, and the weighting of auditory versus visual confidence were all comparable. So their moment-to-moment confidence monitoring appears intact despite lingering auditory deficits and lower self-belief.
papers.abstract: Hearing loss is a widespread condition, affecting more than 15% of the world population. While wearable hearing aids can substantially improve objective hearing quality, it is possible that listeners’ beliefs about their auditory abilities, as well as their subjective confidence in auditory perception remain affected. Such metacognitive underconfidence may then determine whether individuals rely more on auditory versus visual information, form confidence in their perception, and make decisions about the absence of stimuli. Here we compared aided hearing-impaired individuals (N = 15) with matched hearing-unimpaired individuals (N = 17) in an audiovisual detection task in which stimulus intensity was continuously adjusted to hold detection at threshold. Aided hearing-impaired individuals had reduced self-efficacy beliefs about their auditory abilities, with no corresponding reduction in the visual domain. Yet their local metacognition was not different from that of hearing unimpaired individuals: confidence in presence versus absence, the metacognitive evaluation of multisensory stimuli, and the weighting of auditory and visual confidence were all comparable. Together, our results reveal that despite a residual auditory deficit and reduced self-efficacy beliefs about their auditory abilities, local metacognitive monitoring remained unaffected in aided hearing-impaired individuals.

papers.title: Age-related changes in strategy use during reinforcement learning
papers.authors: Irene van de Vijver, Leendert van Maanen
papers.summary: Sixty younger and 59 older adults did a reinforcement learning task where stimulus-response mappings had no structure or could be grouped by semantic or visual regularities, with increasingly explicit hints across four phases. Older adults learned less well, reported using strategies less, and switched to strategy-based responding later. Structure and explicit information helped both age groups, with the biggest gains in older adults and for concrete stimuli, and verbal fluency predicted learning and strategy discovery. The upshot is that age differences in learning reflect not just weaker associative learning but also less spontaneous discovery of useful strategies, which suggests support for strategy discovery could help.
papers.abstract: Age-related declines in reinforcement learning (RL) are commonly attributed to impairments in dopaminergic prediction-error learning and working memory. However, successful RL may also depend on discovering and applying higher-order learning strategies that reduce memory demands. We investigated whether age differences in RL partly reflect reduced spontaneous strategy discovery, whether providing support attenuates these differences, and whether these effects depend on stimulus verbalizability. Sixty younger and 59 older adults completed an RL task in which stimulus-response mappings either contained no underlying structure or could be grouped according to semantic or visual regularities. Across four phases, participants received increasingly explicit information about these regularities. Strategy use was assessed using verbal reports and by fitting sigmoid functions to individual learning curves, estimating the transition to strategy-based responding. Older adults showed lower learning performance, reported using strategies less frequently, and transitioned later to strategy-based responding than younger adults. Providing structured stimulus-response mappings and increasingly explicit information improved learning performance, increased reported strategy use, and accelerated strategy discovery in both age groups, with the largest performance gains observed in older adults and for concrete compared to abstract stimuli. Verbal fluency predicted both learning performance and strategy discovery. These findings suggest that age-related differences in RL reflect not only declines in associative learning but also reduced spontaneous discovery and application of effective learning strategies. Facilitating strategy discovery may therefore represent a promising way to improve learning in older adulthood.

papers.title: GPT-4 reasons like infants about objects but not agents
papers.authors: Alyson Wong, Bill Thompson, Fei Xu
papers.summary: Researchers adapted classic infant experiments on implicit theory of mind so they could be given to GPT-4, using four social reasoning tasks plus a physical reasoning comparison. GPT-4 did very well on the physical reasoning tasks but struggled with the social ones. That suggests domain differences in what the model can do, with a possible weakness in social reasoning that explicit theory-of-mind tests might not reveal.
papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world. However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results. In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM. However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs. The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments. In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4’s implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms. In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2. Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4’s reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4’s social reasoning abilities.

papers.title: Post-Encoding Semantic Processing Produces Systematic Distortions in Episodic Memory
papers.authors: Katelyn G. Cliver, Kennedy King, Alexa Tompary
papers.summary: Across three behavioral experiments, participants learned image locations in a setup that set specific-image memory against general knowledge of where that image's category usually appeared. After learning, they either processed the images at the category level or the item level. Memories that got semantic, category-level processing were less precise and more distorted toward category knowledge than item-level or non-re-exposed ones. Atypical category members were updated more, which suggests that how prior knowledge is organized limits how much new memories change. These results fit the idea that episodic retrieval is constructive.
papers.abstract: How new experiences can update a memory has important consequences for its long-term storage, but little is known about how different kinds of re exposure may differentially influence its content. Inspired by theories of memory reconstruction that posit that memory retrieval depends on the integration of idiosyncratic details and relevant general knowledge, we investigated how exposure to a memory through category- or item-level processing may strengthen its episodic and semantic components. Across three behavioral experiments, participants encoded image-location associations in a protocol designed to generate a conflict between memory for specific images and knowledge of the general location of other images from the same category. Following learning of the locations, participants completed manipulations aimed to prioritize category-level or item-level processing of the images. We hypothesized that requiring semantic processing after learning would reinforce prior category knowledge associated with each image and increase category-driven distortions in memory at test. Our findings revealed that memory for images that underwent semantic processing were less precise and more distorted relative to memories that underwent item-level processing and relative to those that were not re-exposed after encoding. Furthermore, post-encoding manipulations more strongly updated memories of atypical category members, suggesting that the organization of prior knowledge can govern the extent that new memories can be updated. Together, these results highlight the active role of post‑encoding manipulations in differentially reshaping memory content and provide compelling evidence that episodic memory retrieval is a constructive process that integrates across prior knowledge, discrete experiences, and subsequent re-exposure.

papers.title: Age-Related Neural Dedifferentiation Is Driven by Declining Reliability
papers.authors: Tiantian Yang, Molly Simmonite, Ethan Maddox et al.
papers.summary: Neural dedifferentiation, the loss of distinct brain representations with age, is usually measured as within-category similarity (reliability) minus between-category similarity (confusability). Using cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the MiND study, with more than 200 younger and older adults and visual, auditory, and motor cortex, the researchers split the measure into these two parts. Older adults had lower reliability, and that difference was larger than the difference in confusability. Reliability also declined within individuals over about four years. So dedifferentiation appears to come mainly from declining reliability, and reporting distinctiveness alone can hide that.
papers.abstract: Neural dedifferentiation, characterized by reduced distinctiveness of neural representations, is a robust feature of cognitive aging. Multivoxel pattern analyses often operationalize neural distinctiveness as the difference between within-category similarity (reliability) and between-category similarity (confusability). However, it remains unclear whether age-related reductions in distinctiveness are driven by decreases in reliability, increases in confusability, or both, and whether these components demonstrate similar longitudinal trajectories. Using cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) study, we decomposed distinctiveness into its two components across visual, auditory, and motor cortex in more than 200 young (18-29 years) and older adults (65-94 years) and estimated cross-sectional between-person age differences and longitudinal within-person change simultaneously in mixed-effects models. We found that reliability was lower in older vs. younger adults cross-sectionally, and this reduction was significantly larger than the corresponding effect on confusability. Moreover, reliability also declined longitudinally within individuals across a mean interval of four years. These findings indicate that age-related dedifferentiation is driven primarily by declining reliability rather than increasing confusability, and that reporting distinctiveness alone can conceal substantial age-related change in its components. Keywords: Dedifferentiation, distinctiveness, reliability, confusability, aging, longitudinal study

papers.title: Saccade Selection Predictably Changes With Load
papers.authors: Zakaria Gefferie, Estelle Coelingh, Christoph Strauch
papers.summary: The question here is whether choosing where to look works like an economic tradeoff between benefits and costs. Participants chose between saccade targets in directions with known effort costs from pupillometry, while doing a memory task that varied cognitive load. Money could offset the effort costs, and under higher memory load people leaned toward cheaper saccades while reward sensitivity stayed the same. Load also shortened the slowest responses, consistent with less deliberation. Together this supports an economic account of visual selection over pure information maximization.
papers.abstract: Departing from traditional information-maximization accounts, recent work proposes that saccade selection arbitrates economically between the expected benefits and costs of shifting attention. We tested this economic account by manipulating the cognitive resources available during selection, arguing that reduced resources should increase the weight of costs, thereby altering selection. Across two experiments, participants selected between saccade targets while performing a non-spatial memory task that manipulated cognitive load. Targets appeared in directions with previously and independently established intrinsic (effort) costs, quantified through pupillometry. In Experiment 1, monetary rewards were staircased against participants' choices, replicating that money can compensate for intrinsic costs. This yielded an informative reward range from which Experiment 2 sampled randomly. Experiment 2 revealed that higher memory load biased selection toward cost-efficient saccades, while reward sensitivity remained unaffected.Load also selectively shortened the long latency tail, consistent with reduced deliberation under increased load and therefore an increased weight on deliberation cost. Saccade selection thus depends on available cognitive resources, supporting an economic account of visual selection over information maximization accounts.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Theory Unifying Value and Schema in the Prefrontal Cortex
papers.authors: Warren, J., Jensen, K. T., Behrens, T. et al.
papers.summary: The authors build a mechanistic model of prefrontal cortex in which value works as a control signal that gates structured working-memory representations of the current context, rather than just being read out to pick an action. The model carries over to new contexts without further synaptic plasticity, and recurrent neural networks meta-trained with reinforcement or supervised learning end up recreating this same model on value-based tasks. It's an appealing attempt to connect the reinforcement-learning and cognitive-map/schema views of PFC that are usually treated separately.
papers.abstract: Animals exhibit behavioural flexibility by making reward-optimal decisions in unfamiliar situations. Computing value from minimal reward feedback requires leveraging known structure in the world. The Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) plays a pivotal role in both value computation and learning world structure, however mechanistic explanations for each---within the frameworks of Reinforcement Learning and Cognitive Maps---are largely distinct. We develop a mechanistic model of PFC that unifies value and structure through behavioural flexibility. In this model, value acts as a control signal that gates structured working memory representations of the current context in order to ultimately control behaviour. This is a significant departure from the conventional perspective of value, in which it is used for action readout. Critically, this model generalises to novel contexts without the need for additional synaptic plasticity. We demonstrate that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) meta-trained with either reinforcement learning or supervised learning recapitulate this exact model on various value-based tasks. These results not only provide a parsimonious explanation of both the value and schema frameworks of PFC function, but also propose a new mechanistic interpretation of the role of PFC in flexible decision making.

papers.title: A Relational Code for Objects in Primate Frontal Cortex
papers.authors: Watters, N., Gabel, J., Tenenbaum, J. B. et al.
papers.summary: Monkeys held two objects in spatial working memory while the team recorded large populations of neurons in the frontal and supplementary eye fields. Most units were better described by relational tuning (the arrangement of the two objects) than by retinotopic tuning, and the mix of both types supported near-optimal decoding of object locations. A model that integrates receptive fields over potential saccades reproduced the continuum, while averaging and normalization models did not, and the relational code also gave repulsive biases like those seen in behavior.
papers.abstract: When we remember a scene, we recall both the locations of individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Yet, how neurons encode this arrangement alongside individual locations is unknown. In this work, we recorded large-scale neural activity from the frontal and supplementary eye fields of monkeys performing a two-object spatial working-memory task. Using a continuum of two object configurations, we tested whether neurons encoded individual object locations or the spatial relationship between them. Many neurons had well-defined position tuning when a single object was presented. With two objects, responses spanned a continuum from retinotopic to relational tuning. Surprisingly, most units were better explained by relational tuning than retinotopic tuning. Relational and retinotopic units encoded complementary dimensions of the stimulus, and their observed mixture supported near-optimal population decoding of object locations. Relational tuning was systematically aligned with single-object receptive fields, enabling a readout that produced repulsive biases resembling those observed in behavior. Standard multi-object models such as averaging and normalization failed to reproduce the observed continuum, whereas a model integrating receptive fields over potential saccades captured it. These findings show that the frontal oculomotor cortex represents not only where objects are, but also how they are arranged with respect to one another.

papers.title: Effects of within-word consonant similarity in lexical learning
papers.authors: Johanna Basnak, Kenny Smith, Mitsuhiko Ota

papers.title: Revealing contour integration-related ERPs through temporal separation from early visual evoked potentials
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Angeline Y. Yang, Daniel R. Coates et al.
papers.summary: Contour integration ERPs are usually muddied because the contour appears at trial onset, so early visual responses and integration overlap. Here a paradigm separates them in time, and by varying contour fidelity the researchers found an early effect around 100 ms (linked to feature binding) and a late P3b (linked to task effort), alongside the known N200 and N2pc. The occipital N200 behaved differently depending on the manipulation: misaligned elements shrank its amplitude, while oblique orientation delayed it, which fits the idea that it reflects recurrent shape processing.
papers.abstract: Contour integration has been proposed to involve coordinated processing across hierarchical cortical regions. Previous ERP studies have focused primarily on time windows around 200 ms post-contour onset, identifying the occipital N200 and N2pc, which are primarily responsible for visual awareness of integrated shapes and its reliance on spatial attention, respectively. However, findings regarding ERPs at earlier and later stages, as well as how contour properties modulate ERPs related to contour integration, remain unclear. This gap largely stems from traditional paradigms presenting contours at trial onset, confounding early visual evocation with contour integration. To resolve this, we employed a paradigm that temporally dissociates the two processes. By varying contour fidelity, we identified two additional components alongside the occipital N200 and N2pc: an early effect (~100 ms) reflecting feature binding and a late P3b component reflecting task-related effort. Furthermore, the occipital N200 was differentially modulated by contour fidelity and detectability: reducing fidelity through misalignment of contour components decreased its amplitude without affecting latency, whereas reducing detectability through oblique orientation increased latency without affecting amplitude. These findings suggest that the occipital N200 reflects recurrent shape processing, a crucial step in which attended, bound features are integrated into a coherent visual representation that enters conscious awareness, shedding light on how hierarchical processes cooperate dynamically to integrate local elements into a global percept.

papers.title: Morphological analysis when morphemes are hard to detect: Evidence from infixation and reduplication
papers.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado, Kathleen Rastle
papers.summary: Most evidence for morphological analysis in reading comes from English suffixes, which look about the same from word to word. Using a morpheme interference task in Tagalog, the researchers tested infixes (like the -in- in t-in-awag) and reduplicants (like ta- in ta tawag), where the surface form is less consistent. Nonwords with morphological structure still led to lower accuracy and slower responses, so skilled readers seem to detect these trickier morphemes too, which pushes theories of morpheme learning to account for them.
papers.abstract: There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars ( clean in cleaner, cleanliness ; -ed in walked , jumped ). It remains unclear whether morphological analysis is also robust when morphemes lack a consistent surface form. Using the morpheme interference paradigm in Tagalog, we test whether infixes and reduplicants are detected during prelexical processing. Infixes are inserted within a stem and therefore reduce the consistency of its surface realisation (e.g., tawag → t-in-awag ‘called’), while reduplicants involve partial or full copying of a stem and therefore lack a consistent surface realisation (e.g., tawag and lundag become ta tawag ‘will call’ and lu lundag ‘will jump’, where ta- and lu- are instances of the same reduplicant morpheme). We found robust morpheme interference effects in both accuracy and RTs. Specifically, nonwords with morphological structure induced significantly lower accuracy and longer RTs than nonwords without. Our findings show skilled readers’ acquired sensitivity to these sophisticated morphological structures and motivate refinements to theories of morpheme learning.

papers.title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
papers.authors: Mengmi Zhang, Elisa Pavarino, Xiao Liu et al.

papers.title: The spatial area of the normalization pool in early visual processing
papers.authors: Aqsa Hassan, Felix A. Wichmann, Rafal K. Mantiuk et al.
papers.summary: To pin down how far visual masking interactions reach across space, the researchers ran forced-choice masking experiments with a small Gabor target on masks of varying size, at several spatial frequencies and at the fovea, 5° and 10° eccentricity. In the periphery, thresholds rose with mask size and then leveled off, and fitting divisive normalization gave a Gaussian pool about 0.65° wide for 1 cycle/degree that shrank in proportion to spatial frequency, regardless of eccentricity or mask contrast. The fovea was the surprise: mask size made no difference to thresholds even though the mask clearly raised them, and that remains unexplained.
papers.abstract: Precisely measuring the properties of low-level visual processing is of theoretical interest as such properties often generalize to other processing in the brain and have immediate applications for image and video processing. The initial stages of human visual processing split the signal into spatial frequency and orientation-tuned channels, which interact nonlinearly, are typically modeled as divisive normalization. While we know in detail which spatial frequency and orientation channels interact, we know much less about how far the interactions reach across space. In particular, we lack psychophysical data to constrain the spatial area of the normalization pool. To provide such constraints, we set up forced choice masking experiments varying the size of the mask while we keep the spatial frequency and orientation of the mask the same as the targets. The target grating was always a small (0.5 cycles standard deviation) circular Gabor centrally superimposed over 15% and 40% contrast masks. We tested eight different mask sizes for 1, 2, and 4 cycles per degree vertical stimuli in the fovea and at 5° and 10° eccentricities.
