In the periphery at 5° and 10° eccentricities, contrast thresholds increase with increasing mask size and then saturate as expected, which allows us to estimate the spatial extent of the normalization pool by fitting a divisive normalization model. The fitted Gaussian normalization pool has a standard deviation of 0.65° for 1 cycle per degree gratings and scaled inversely proportional to the spatial frequency of the gratings. Neither the eccentricity nor the mask contrast influenced the size of the normalization pool. In the fovea, however, the size of the mask had no influence on thresholds, even though the mask reliably elevated thresholds. Thus, we are left with an accurate estimate of normalization pool sizes in the periphery, along with the unresolved question of why masking in the fovea shows a different behavior.

papers.title: Competitive Neural Dynamics of Flicker-Induced Time Dilation
papers.authors: Aarthi Venkatesh, Rakesh Sengupta
papers.summary: People judged durations of flickering stimuli at 20, 30 and 40 Hz, and faster flicker made things seem longer, with the point of subjective equality shifting by more than 90 ms in the most extreme condition. The team then used an existing on-center off-surround recurrent network, mapping flicker density to the input level of its nodes, and its winner-take-all dynamics reproduced the non-linear time expansion. The suggestion is that the same competitive mechanism could account for both novelty-driven and flicker-driven time dilation.
papers.abstract: Time’s Subjective Expansion (TSE) is a phenomenon where salient or dynamic stimuli are perceived as lasting longer than static or less dynamic counterparts. While previous work has modeled this in oddball paradigms using habituation dynamics, it remains unclear if the same neural mechanisms account for distortions caused by visual flicker. In this study, we conducted a temporal comparison experiment using asynchronous flickering stimuli at 20Hz, 30Hz, and 40Hz. Behavioral results demonstrate a robust, frequency-dependent time dilation effect: 40Hz stimuli are perceived as significantly longer than 20Hz stimuli, with the Point of Subjective Equality (PSE) shifting by over 90ms inthe extreme condition. We apply a previously established On Center Off-Surround (OCOS) recurrent neural network model to these findings. We demonstrate that by mapping flicker density to the input clamping level (I) of the network nodes, the inherent Winner-Take-All (WTA) dynamics naturally reproduce the observed non-linear expansion of time. This suggests a unified computational mechanism where time perception is an emergent property of competitive neural dynamics, modulated equally by novelty (habituation) and sensory density (flicker).

papers.title: Gradual Extinction via US Intensity Reduction: a Translational Test of Fear Memory Updating in Humans
papers.authors: Francesco Tortora, Ebru Ecem Tavacioglu, Yannik Stegmann et al.
papers.summary: Fear often returns after exposure therapy, possibly because extinction forms a separate memory instead of updating the original one. Following rodent work, the researchers tested in 60 people whether gradually lowering the shock intensity during extinction, rather than removing it abruptly, reduces the return of fear. Self-reported fear and heart rate didn't differ between groups, but electrodermal responses during spontaneous recovery were smaller after gradual extinction, so the support for the animal findings is only partial and depends on the response measure.
papers.abstract: Relapse of fear-related symptoms after exposure-based treatment remains a major challenge across anxiety disorders. One potential explanation is that extinction learning yields a new memory trace rather than being integrated with the original fear memory, allowing fear to resurface. Building on recent research in rodents, we tested whether gradually reducing the intensity of the unconditioned stimulus (US) during extinction attenuates the return of fear in humans by promoting the integration of extinction learning into existing fear memories. Using a two-day fear-conditioning paradigm, 60 participants underwent differential fear acquisition, in which one stimulus (conditioned stimulus, CS+) was paired with an aversive electric stimulation (US), while another stimulus (CS−) was never paired. Participants were then randomly assigned to either classic extinction (CE), in which no US was delivered, or gradual extinction (GE), in which the US intensity was progressively reduced across blocks. On the second day, fear memory was assessed using spontaneous recovery and reinstatement tests. Subjective fear ratings and heart rate responses were comparable between extinction procedures. In contrast, during spontaneous recovery, electrodermal responses were larger in the CE group than in the GE group, with heightened responses to both CS+ and CS−. Overall, our findings provide partial support for the translation of gradual extinction effects observed in animal models to humans. While effects differed across response systems, the attenuated electrodermal recovery following gradual extinction suggests that progressively reducing US intensity to minimize prediction errors may alter the subsequent expression of fear memories. These findings highlight gradual US-intensity reduction as a promising translational approach for investigating mechanisms underlying fear relapse in humans.

papers.title: Idiosyncratic random behavior in a massive online sample
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Sami Ryan Yousif
papers.summary: Over 50,000 people produced short random sequences (8-12 responses) of coin flips, dice rolls and grid locations. Individuals were consistent across the three tasks, in both their sequence features and a simple computational model, which argues that randomness comes partly from idiosyncratic processes and not just shared heuristics. Because the sequences were so short, differences in working memory or attention are less likely to explain this.
papers.abstract: What factors govern and predict an individual’s random behavior? Under many views, human random behavior arises from a grab bag of group-level heuristics (e.g., the representativeness heuristic, the law of small numbers, etc.). Contrary to this view, we present evidence that random behavior arises from highly idiosyncratic processes, borne out even with minimal amounts of data. Over 50,000 people generated random sequences of (a) coin flips, (b) dice rolls, and (c) locations in a 3-by-3 grid. Importantly, participants submitted only 8-12 responses in each task. This very small window minimizes many factors that might create individual differences in random behavior on their own, such as differences in working memory or attention. Yet, individuals demonstrated consistent behavior across these three different tasks, as reflected both by their sequence features and by a simple computational model of random behavior. Thus, these results indicate that, while some general heuristics guide random behavior, there also exist unique, idiosyncratic patterns that warrant attention — raising broader questions about how random behavior is realized in the human mind.

papers.title: The Neural Correlates of Implicit Emotion Regulation through Affect Labeling as Reflected in EEG
papers.authors: Jinyu Chen, Johanna M.P. Baas, Leon Kenemans et al.
papers.summary: Affect labeling (putting a word to your emotion) calms people in the moment, but whether it has lasting effects is unclear. With EEG, the researchers compared it to affect matching and to feature labeling, re-exposing participants to negative images immediately and after 15 minutes. Negative images produced the expected larger late positive potential, more theta power and more right-hemisphere alpha, but none of these measures showed an effect of labeling, so there is no sign of a lasting benefit, though effects during the intervention itself may have been missed.
papers.abstract: Affect labeling reduces emotional responses during and immediately after use, but evidence for lasting regulatory effects remains mixed. While there is no experiential evidence for lasting effects, psychophysiological studies do hint at a longer-lasting impact. However, neuroimaging research has mainly compared affect labeling with affect matching. Although both involve emotional processing, affect labeling additionally engages linguistic processing. Thus, it remains unclear whether observed neural differences reflect emotion-focused labeling or mere linguistic processing, and whether such effects endure over time. We recorded EEG to examine the effects of affect labeling on negative emotion across two re-exposure phases: immediate and after a short interval (15 minutes). Affect labeling (emotion-specific words) was compared with affect matching (emotion-focused perceptual processing) and feature labeling (linguistic processing without emotional content), allowing us to dissociate emotional and linguistic components. Event-related potentials and EEG oscillatory activity were analyzed in both phases, with pre-intervention neural responses included as baseline. Robust emotion-related neural activity was observed. Negative (vs. neutral) stimuli elicited increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes, enhanced fronto-central-parietal theta power, and greater right-hemispheric alpha activity. However, LPP, theta-, and alpha-band power did not show effects of affect labeling compared to the control conditions. Thus, the present findings provide no evidence for a lasting labeling effect. Because we focused on re-exposure, we may have missed potential regulatory effects during the intervention itself. Future research should further identify factors that influence the effectiveness of labeling and clarify when this implicit emotion regulation pathway is engaged.

papers.title: Bilingualism and Cognitive Ageing: Domain-Specific Benefits After Controlling for Education and Lifestyle
papers.authors: Xinyu Liu, Umit Aydin, Christos Pliatsikas
papers.summary: Using the Cam-CAN dataset of adults aged 18-88, the researchers compared monolinguals and bilinguals and also modeled bilingual experience as a continuous measure, controlling for factors like education. Bilinguals showed better-preserved fluid reasoning in older age and higher verbal abstraction scores, while multitasking showed no such benefit in the summary. The pattern suggests bilingual advantages may appear specifically in older age and in particular cognitive domains.
papers.abstract: Lifelong bilingualism has been proposed as a cognitively enriching experience that mitigates age-related declines in cognitive abilities; however, the evidence remains mixed due to issues such as small samples, absence of effects in younger samples, and not accounting for confounding factors (e.g. education). Here we address these issues by examining adults aged 18-88 from the Cam-CAN dataset in two ways: by comparing monolinguals to bilinguals (N=390) and by examining bilingual experience as a continuous factor with a newly devised metric (N=460). Generalised additive models assessed fluid reasoning, ecological multitasking, and verbal abstraction. Increased age was associated with declined fluid reasoning and multitasking, but better verbal abstraction. Compared to monolinguals, bilinguals showed better preserved fluid reasoning in older age, suggesting decelerated cognitive decline, and higher verbal abstraction scores. Our results help refine theories on the effects of bilingualism on cognition by showcasing that are likely to emerge in older age only.

papers.title: Dream incorporation and subsequent memory change after learning and waking reactivation
papers.authors: María Laura Gorosito, Matias Rodolfo Pretel, Nerea L. Herrero et al.
papers.summary: Fifteen participants learned word-definition-image associations over four days at home, with dream reports collected after serial awakenings, once after learning and again after an incomplete reminder that reactivated the memory. After initial learning, more explicit task-related dream content went with greater improvement in word recall, but after reactivation it went with lower memory change for words and definitions. This exploratory result hints that what dreams reveal about memory processing may depend on the memory's state before sleep.
papers.abstract: Dreams often incorporate recent waking experiences, but whether the relationship between dream content and subsequent memory depends on the state of the memory before sleep remains unclear. In this exploratory study, fifteen participants learned novel word-definition-image associations across a four-day home-based protocol. Dream reports were collected after serial awakenings following initial learning and again after an incomplete reminder designed to reactivate the memory. Dream incorporations were classified as explicit, comprising recognizable references to the learned material or experimental procedure, or semantic/thematic, reflecting conceptual associations with the learned material. Following initial learning, greater explicit task-related dream incorporation was associated with greater subsequent improvement in word recall. In contrast, following memory reactivation, greater explicit and total task-related incorporation was associated with lower subsequent memorychange scores for both words and definitions. Phase-by-incorporation analyses confirmed that this relationship differed between phases for word recall, whereas the corresponding interactions for definition recall did not reach significance. These findings suggest that the relationship between dream incorporation and later memory may depend on the state of the memory before sleep, and that dream reports may provide a behavioral window into both post-learning and post-reactivation memory processing.

papers.title: Shared and Distinct Neural Correlates of Reading and Writing in Chinese and Alphabetic Scripts: A Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Luchang Qiao, Jie Chen, Siyi Fan et al.
papers.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 138 reading and 36 writing neuroimaging experiments, then split them by alphabetic and Chinese scripts. Reading and writing shared a mostly left-lateralized frontoparietal network, while reading leaned on left inferior frontal, temporal and ventral occipitotemporal regions and writing on frontoparietal and sensorimotor ones. The patterns also differed by script, for instance in left IOG and SPL for Chinese, and connectivity and decoding analyses placed these regions in partly overlapping functional systems.
papers.abstract: Reading and writing are closely related literacy skills that draw on partially shared orthographic and linguistic representations while differing in their perceptual and motor demands. Although robust behavioral associations between reading and writing have been established, the extent to which they share neural substrates, whether these neural relationships vary across writing systems, and how the involved regions are embedded within broader functional systems remain unclear. In the current study, we conducted Activation Likelihood Estimation (ALE) meta-analyses of 138 reading and 36 writing experiments, followed by conjunction and contrast analyses to identify shared and domain-preferential neural convergence between reading and writing. We further conducted the same analyses separately in alphabetic (67 reading, 25 writing experiments) and Chinese (71 reading, 11 writing experiments) datasets to examine how these patterns vary across writing systems. To characterize the functional profiles of representative regions identified by the ALE analyses, we conducted Meta-Analytic Connectivity Modeling (MACM) to delineate their coactivation patterns, examined their spatial overlap with 14 canonical functional networks, and performed whole-map functional decoding using Neurosynth. Across writing systems, reading and writing showed a shared, predominantly left-lateralized neural organization centered on frontoparietal regions, alongside domain-preferential convergence in left inferior frontal, temporal, and ventral occipitotemporal regions for reading and in frontoparietal and sensorimotor regions for writing. These patterns also varied across writing systems. For example, the left MTG (overall reading-preferential), left IOG (Chinese reading-writing shared), left PreCG (alphabetic writing-preferential), and left SPL (Chinese writing-preferential) represented distinct patterns of shared and preferential involvement in reading and writing. The MACM and functional characterization results indicated that these regions were embedded within differentiated but partially overlapping large-scale functional systems, with distinct functional profiles spanning linguistic-semantic, visual-orthographic, sensorimotor, and visuospatial functions. Together, these findings provide a quantitative account of the shared and domain-preferential neural organization of reading and writing and its variation between the Chinese and alphabetic literatures.

papers.title: Right Error Wrong Time: Condition-Dependent Fast and Slow Errors Distort Architecture Inference in Systems Factorial Technology
papers.authors: Hang Qian, Paul Michael Garrett, Philip L. Smith et al.
papers.summary: Systems Factorial Technology infers processing architecture from response times, but usually only from correct responses. Diffusion-model simulations showed that when errors differ in how common and how fast or slow they are across conditions, the survivor interaction contrast gets distorted: a coactive signature can start to look like parallel self-terminating processing. Conditional accuracy functions are suggested as a practical companion check for this risk.
papers.abstract: Systems Factorial Technology infers processing architecture from response-time distributions obtained under factorial manipulations of information quality. These analysis are conventionally restricted to correct responses, leaving unclear whether condition-dependent errors can distort the architecture-diagnostic survivor interaction contrast (SIC). We used diffusion-model simulations to examine whether SIC-based diagnoses remain valid when errors differ in prevalence and timing across the high–high, high–low, low–high, and low–low conditions. We first implemented coactive processing using the partitioned circular diffusion model under AND and OR task rules. Cross-trial variability in drift magnitude produced slow errors, whereas variability in the decision boundary produced fast errors. Although the expected stochastic ordering of the correct-response survivor functions was generally preserved, both mechanisms progressively attenuated the characteristic negative-then-positive coactive SIC, causing it to resemble the entirely positive signature of parallel self-terminating processing. We then generalized the analysis to a parallel self-terminating architecture implemented using linear-drift, linear-infinitesimal-variance model. Racing generated slow errors even without cross-trial drift-rate variability, but the expected positive SIC remained robust while the error pattern was relatively similar across factorial conditions. Adding drift-rate variability differentiated the condition-specific error patterns and progressively weakened the SIC. These findings show that presence of errors compromises architectural diagnosis when their timing and prevalence differ across four factorial conditions, causing correct-response selection to reshape the contributing RT distributions unequally. Conditional accuracy functions provide a practical companion measure for identifying this risk.

papers.title: From structured knowledge to flexible behaviour: the importance of local prefrontal computations
papers.authors: Mohamady El-Gaby, Kris Jensen, Svenja Kuechenhoff et al.
papers.summary: Instead of treating the prefrontal cortex mainly as a controller that directs sensory-action mappings elsewhere, this review argues that much of the flexible computation happens locally within it. The proposed framework, duplicated and structured representations, has prefrontal neurons encode combinations of action and context, with the world's abstract structure built into the connections between them. The authors say it accounts for sequence working memory, planning and value-based decisions, and could extend to hierarchical reasoning and social computation.
papers.abstract: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) transforms what we know about the world into intelligent, adaptive behaviour. Existing theories have traditionally explained this function through cross-circuit interactions, where PFC neurons control sensory-action mappings elsewhere in the brain. However, recent findings reveal a remarkable organisation of neuronal activity that enables flexible computation within the PFC itself. These findings motivate a framework of duplicated and structured representations (DSRs), where the abstract structure of the world is embedded locally in connections between prefrontal neurons encoding conjunctions of action and context. We review an extensive body of empirical findings showing that DSRs explain canonical PFCdependent behaviours as diverse as sequence working memory, planning, and value-guided decisions. In each case, PFC neurons represent multiple actions simultaneously. Structured connectivity between these action representations then guides local network dynamics to infer how behaviour should be organised - simplifying both computation and readout. Taken further, the same logic offers a mechanistic foothold on some of the PFC's most elusive functions, including hierarchical reasoning and social computations. Overall, the DSR framework provides a unified understanding of prefrontal computations and a tractable basis for a new generation of mechanistic research.

papers.title: Day by Day, Bit by Bit: Knowledge Building Mechanisms Evolve with Development
papers.authors: Layla Unger, Olivera Savic, Vladimir Sloutsky
papers.summary: Four- to six-year-olds were exposed to regularities among words repeatedly over a month, to see whether they build up connected word knowledge across encounters. Younger children seemed to relearn the regularities from scratch each time, while older children's connections got stronger with each exposure. So the way kids accumulate knowledge over time seems to change quite a bit during these early years.
papers.abstract: Much of human knowledge distills patterns that are consistent across many similar experiences over time, such as the typical layout of a bedroom. This is particularly true of word knowledge. The thousands of words we learn form a stable, interconnected network of word meanings that capture regularities in the way words are typically combined to express ideas, such as that “oranges” are something you can “eat” and similar to “apples”. Yet, we know surprisingly little about accumulating knowledge from regularities over time, especially in childhood when building knowledge is paramount. Here, we investigated 4-6-year-old children’s abilities to accumulate interconnected word knowledge from regularities experienced repeatedly over a month. Younger children appeared to relearn the regularities anew at each exposure, whereas older children accumulated increasingly strong connections across encounters. These findings point to substantial developmental changes in gradual learning processes that build knowledge over time.

papers.title: Impaired Updating and Maintenance of Latent Structural Associations Underlie Cognitive Inflexibility along an Obsessive–Compulsive Dimension
papers.authors: Georgios Tertikas, Nadescha Trudel, Tricia Xing Fang Seow et al.
papers.summary: A new structural inference task separated three things that could underlie cognitive inflexibility in obsessive-compulsive symptoms: learning associations, updating beliefs after the structure changes, and inferring associations never directly observed. In a general-population sample of 313 people, higher OC symptoms went with poorer updating and weaker generalisation to unobserved associations, while initial learning was fine. In the fMRI sample (N=51), the medial orbitofrontal cortex overrepresented irrelevant associations and the posterior hippocampus was worse at forming new latent ones, so the problem looks like a failure to revise a model rather than to learn one.
papers.abstract: Impaired cognitive flexibility, the ability to form and update latent structural associations, is a hallmark of psychiatric conditions such as obsessive-compulsive (OC) disorder, yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a novel structural inference task, we dissociated three candidate mechanisms: (i) initial acquisition of associative structures, (ii) belief updating following structural changes, and (iii) inference about unobserved associations. In a large general-population sample (N=313), transdiagnostically characterised OC symptoms were linked to impaired updating following structural change and reduced generalisation to unobserved associations, whilst initial learning remained intact. Using fMRI (N=51), we found this was driven by overrepresenting structurally irrelevant associations in medial orbitofrontal cortex, and impaired formation of novel latent associations in posterior hippocampus. These findings reveal that OC-related cognitive inflexibility is grounded in dissociable fronto-hippocampal representational failures that impair structural model revision, rather than the capacity to acquire latent associations in the first place.

papers.title: The Role of Prior Knowledge in Epistemic Curiosity Across Adulthood
papers.authors: Mats Abrahamse, Alexandr Ten, Kou Murayama et al.
papers.summary: Older adults tend to stay curious despite declines in curiosity-related personality traits, and the researchers tested whether their richer prior knowledge explains that. In two experiments (216 people each), knowledge strongly drove curiosity regardless of age, and when the experiments pitted knowledge against age, older adults were more curious in domains where they knew more and less curious where younger adults knew more. Knowledge differences mediated these effects, so some earlier reports of age differences in curiosity may really be about what people already know.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that older adults maintain high levels of state curiosity when presented with epistemic materials, despite age-related declines in personality traits related to curiosity. We hypothesized that this age-related preservation in state curiosity is explained by older adults’ rich prior knowledge, given that knowledge acts as a key driver of state curiosity across the adult lifespan. To test this idea, we conducted two experiments that examined older and younger adults’ curiosity to learn the answers to questions in low- and high-knowledge domains. Experiment 1 (N = 216) used learning materials characterized by large population-level differences in prior knowledge, but limited variation across age groups. The results showed that prior knowledge substantially affects state curiosity, irrespective of age, while the effect of age on state curiosity was minimal. Experiment 2 (N = 216) explicitly accounted for age differences in knowledge by orthogonalizing the effects of knowledge and age. We found that relative to younger adults, older adults experienced stronger curiosity for high-knowledge domains, whereas in other domains where younger adults were more knowledgeable, older adults experienced weaker curiosity relative to younger adults. Such age-related differences in curiosity were mediated by age-related differences in knowledge. These findings point to the important role of prior knowledge in curiosity across younger and older adults, extending theoretical notions on curiosity. Our results also suggest that previously observed age differences in state curiosity might be partly attributable to age-related differences in knowledge.

papers.title: Examining the correspondence between quantitative measures of episodic content and phenomenology of past and future autobiographical thoughts
papers.authors: Lucie Reed, Andrew David Lawrence, Lisa Evans
papers.summary: Across two studies (n = 52 and 82), young adults recalled autobiographical memories and imagined future events, rated how vivid they were and how much they felt they were (pre)living them, and had their narratives scored for episodic detail. Trial-by-trial mixed-effects models showed that subjective ratings and episodic content were meaningfully linked, mostly through event details and emotion/thought details, and the link was a bit stronger for imagined futures than for memories. That pushes back on earlier claims that the two are distinct aspects of remembering, though content doesn't fully determine how the experience feels.
papers.abstract: Memories for the personal past and imaginings of the future can be examined via the participant’s subjective experience or a quantitative assessment of their episodic content. There is ongoing debate as to the relationship between these measures. Here we conducted two independent studies (n = 52 and 82) in healthy young adults who were presented with several cue words to prompt recollection of autobiographical memories and imaginings of possible future events. They subsequently rated each of these experiences for its overall vividness and their sense of (p)reliving it. The episodic content of each narrative was scored by the experimenter according to a standardised system (Autobiographical Interview; Levine et al., 2002). Linear mixed-effects modelling, which can examine relationships on a trial-by-trial basis, revealed a significant association between subjective ratings and experimenter-scored episodic content in both studies. Further analysis revealed that within the episodic content category, the subcategories of event details (e.g. actions, people and objects, which are related to the narrative unfolding of events), and emotion/thought details were the primary ones significantly related to both the sense of vividness and (p)reliving. Alignment tended to be stronger when imaging the future than recalling the past. Our findings refute strong previous claims, based on suboptimal analyses, that quantitative measures of content and subjective ratings are distinct aspects of remembering. Thus, episodic content meaningfully aligns with, but does not fully determine, subjective experiences of vividness and (p)reliving. Further research is now required to determine the factors which might moderate this link.

papers.title: Predictors of Reading and Spelling ability in adults: Phonological skills outweigh Visual Attention Span
papers.authors: Jennifer Burt, Jo-Maree Ceccato, Jack Mitchell Ingram Leggett
papers.summary: Some argue that visual attention span, the ability to pick out letters from a brief string, supports reading independently of phonological skill. With a new low-memory-load test alongside a traditional one, 264 adults were measured on reading, spelling, phonology and print exposure. Two phonological measures explained over 30% of literacy variance beyond visual attention span, while each attention span measure uniquely explained at most 3%, so its causal role in literacy looks minor at best.
papers.abstract: According to the Visual attention span (VAS) hypothesis, the ability to identify a briefly presented sequence of visual elements (usually consonants) aids reading acquisition independently of skills related to the sounds of a language (phonology). A new test with a reduced memory load addressed concerns about a phonological memory confound in traditional VAS tests. In this PreProbe test, a probe letter was presented before each trial and the task was to decide whether it occurred in the brief five-letter sequence. A correlational study with 264 adults assessed the relationships of VAS, phonological skills, and print exposure with both word-reading and spelling. Both PreProbe and the traditional partial report VAS (PosProbe) had modest correlations with the literacy measures, and also with the measures of phonological skills. In regression analyses, two phonological measures explained over 30% of literacy variance independently of VAS, while each VAS measure uniquely explained a maximum of 3%. VAS may reflect achievement in phonological and literacy skills, and has at best a minor causal role in literacy.

papers.title: CortexLens: Systematically Decoding Interpretable Visual Patterns from Human Visual Cortex
papers.authors: Qinglin Qi, Yiming Tang, Lu Mi et al.
papers.summary: CortexLens is a framework for finding interpretable visual features in fMRI responses, using Matryoshka sparse autoencoders on each visual region and a vision-language model to label the patterns. A separate low-level stream recovers thousands of interpretable features from early visual areas, where earlier language-based methods found few, and the high-level stream finds semantic features that carry over to BOLD5000. It also flags a pitfall: a low-level feature that co-varies with a salient semantic one can get mislabeled as the semantic one.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain encodes visual information remains a fundamental challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Sparse dictionary learning (SDL) has recently been applied to fMRI to discover visual features represented in the visual cortex. Existing approaches, however, depend on a vision-language model to identify the feature at discovery, and report limited discovery of the low-level visual features processed in early retinotopic visual regions that play an essential role in human visual cognition. We propose an automatic framework that systematically discovers visual features encoded in the human visual cortex, encompassing both high-level and low-level visual features. The framework decomposes fMRI responses across the full visual hierarchy with Matryoshka sparse autoencoders applied per region of interest, interprets the resulting fMRI activity patterns with a vision-language model, and introduces a set of feature channels to recover the low-level visual features that language-based interpretation fails to capture. On the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and on the Brain Encoder Generated Dataset (BEGD), a separate set of synthesized responses from a transformer brain encoder, the low-level stream recovers thousands of interpretable low-level visual features from early retinotopic visual regions, where prior language-based pipelines report limited discovery. The high-level stream recovers interpretable semantic visual features on both datasets and generalizes to BOLD5000. Our analysis further reveals a systematic confound in language-based interpretation: fMRI activity patterns whose true representation is a low-level visual feature can be misidentified as a semantic visual feature when that feature co-varies with a salient semantic visual feature.

papers.title: Suppressing Distractors, Enhancing Targets: Template Tuning in Ensemble Perception
papers.authors: Gizem Tanseli Kaspar, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth
papers.summary: Participants did a colour-based visual search and then estimated the average orientation of a group of items in which those target and distractor colours came back. Estimates were biased by the target template, most strongly when both colours reappeared together, and that combined bias was bigger than the sum of the target and distractor effects alone. Showing the display for 500 ms rather than 150 ms made responses more precise but didn't change the size of the bias.
papers.abstract: AbstractEnsemble perception is a fundamental mechanism enabling the visual system to rapidly extract summary statistical properties (e.g., mean orientation) from a large number of objects. This study investigated the influence of attentional templates for targets and distractors which are formed during visual search, on subsequent ensemble perception. Participants first completed a visual search task involving target and distractor colors, followed by an ensemble orientation estimation task in which these colors recurred in various combinations. The first experiment revealed that target template systematically biased ensemble estimates, with the strongest effect occurring when both template colors recurred together. Furthermore, on these trials the bias exceeded the sum of the individual effects of target and distractor conditions, which demonstrates that combined effect of target enhancement and distractor suppression may be greater than predicted by their individual effects. In the second experiment, presentation duration (150 ms vs. 500 ms) was manipulated. While our results showed that duration did not alter the magnitude of the biases, a longer presentation time improved response precision. These findings suggest that ensemble perception can be modulated by recently formed attentional templates and systematically shape the formation of summary statistical representations.Keywords: Ensemble Perception, Attentional Templates, Statistical Summary Representations

papers.title: The use of Grammatical Gender in Predictive language comprehension: Evidence from Young and Older adults
papers.authors: Anurag Anurag, Niharika Singh
papers.summary: Using eye-tracking, younger and older Hindi speakers heard sentences with a gendered adjective and looked at pictures to show whether they anticipated the upcoming noun. Early on, both groups looked equally at the target and at a competitor that fit the adjective's meaning but not its gender. Somewhat later, looks to the target began to edge out the gender-mismatched competitor. Nothing differed by age, so meaning seems to drive early prediction, with gender coming in later, and neither declines in simple sentences.
papers.abstract: Prediction-by-association, in which a word pre-activates lexically associated words, is thought to be relatively automatic and therefore spared in healthy aging. In languages with grammatical gender, however, prenominal modifiers carry both semantic and gender information, so it remains unclear whether older adults also use morphosyntactic agreement to anticipate upcoming words. We tested whether younger (n = 32, 20–35 years) and older (n = 31, 55–75 years) native Hindi speakers use the meaning and the gender marking of a prenominal adjective to anticipate an upcoming noun. In a visual-world eye-tracking task, participants heard sentences such as Abhi aap ek nukili wali sui dekhenge ('Now you will see a pointed needle') while viewing a target (needle), an adjective competitor that was semantically compatible with the adjective but mismatched its gender (spear), and two unrelated distractors. In both age groups, the target and the adjective competitor attracted comparable anticipatory fixations shortly after the adjective onset, and both were fixated more than the distractors. Later in the pre-noun interval, fixations to the target began to exceed those to the gender-mismatching competitor, although this advantage was modest. None of these effects interacted with age group, and filler sentences without a predictive adjective elicited no anticipatory fixations. These findings suggest that early anticipation is driven primarily by lexical-semantic association, with grammatical gender constraining predictions somewhat later, and that neither source of information shows age-related decline in contextually simple sentences.Keywords: prediction; aging; grammatical gender; visual world paradigm; eye-tracking; Hindi

papers.title: Speech Monitoring During Self-Comprehension
papers.authors: Andreas Lind, Petter Johansson, Lars Hall
papers.summary: Rather than assuming speakers catch their own errors through pre-articulatory monitoring or forward-model predictions, this account says error detection falls out of self-comprehension, where people understand their own speech as it unfolds. Anticipation comes from multi-scale pattern completion and from anticipatory coarticulation, which gives auditory and somatosensory hints about upcoming sounds before they are produced. The authors propose three routes to detecting errors, which they say can explain the range of interruption latencies, including very fast ones, and reinterpret findings on noise-masked feedback and cortical attenuation during speaking.
papers.abstract: Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors. Speakers’ ability to detect errors and other problems in their own speech is commonly explained by monitoring mechanisms that rely on pre-articulatory representations, production states, or derivative predictions. We develop an alternative, cue-integrative account in which verbal self-monitoring is a natural consequence of what we have previously termed self-comprehension: speakers’ integration of contextual and sensory information to understand their own unfolding speech without requiring that meaning or intention be fully specified before articulation. Two sources of anticipatory information are central to the account, neither requiring explicit predictive or forward-model representations. First, we apply to self-comprehension the recently proposed idea of multi-scale pattern completion during speech comprehension, which allows partial input to activate continuations at multiple linguistic levels, generating contextually constrained anticipation. Second, anticipatory coarticulation can provide auditory and somatosensory information about upcoming speech before the relevant segment is produced, challenging the assumption that sensory feedback is too slow for online self-comprehension. We propose three routes to error detection: divergence between pattern-completion-based and coarticulatory anticipations; divergence between pattern-completion-based anticipation and post-articulatory sensory feedback; and post-articulatory self-comprehension in the absence of sufficiently informative anticipation. These routes provide a framework for explaining error detection across the observed range of error-interruption latencies, including very rapid interruptions. This framework also provides alternative interpretations of error-detection findings under noise-masked auditory feedback and of cortical attenuation during speaking without requiring a separate pre-articulatory monitoring channel, explicit predictions, or prediction-error computations.

papers.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made
papers.authors: Caitlin Lloyd, Zarrar Shehzad, Janet Schebendach et al.
papers.summary: In a large online sample (N = 1,052), people rated foods and made choices, and a drift diffusion model captured the decision process. Three attributes (tastiness, healthiness and umami) all shaped choices, and healthier choosers were more often women, higher in eating restraint, or lower in BMI. Healthier choices didn't depend only on self-control, because these people also saw healthy foods as tastier, and high-restraint people deliberated less, which suggests more automatic choosing. So there are several routes to eating healthily, and it doesn't always mean giving up taste.
papers.abstract: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

papers.title: Information-Seeking Behavior in Mice (Mus musculus) During Visual Discriminations: Evaluating Metacognitive and Alternative Accounts in a Target-Cueing Paradigm
papers.authors: Yuya Hataji, Kazuhiro Goto
papers.summary: Mice could ask for a hint about where a rewarded stimulus was during visual discrimination tasks, which tests whether information seeking reflects metacognition. Some training results fit that idea, since hints helped most when discriminations were harder, but critical tests didn't: mice often sought hints when none were needed and did so less when the display was uninformative. Information seeking therefore seems driven by several factors, including competition, reinforcement history and the hint's usefulness, rather than confidence monitoring alone.
papers.abstract: Information-seeking behavior is often interpreted as evidence of metacognitive monitoring, but nonmetacognitive factors may also explain such behavior. We examined this issue in miceusing a target-cueing procedure in which an information-seeking response produced a hint indicating the location of the rewarded stimulus. In Experiment 1, mice performed an orientation discrimination. In Experiment 2, the same mice performed a grating discrimination in which grating coarseness varied across trials. During training, some aspects of performancewere compatible with a metacognitive account. In Experiment 1, information seeking did not increase reliably as the discrimination became more difficult, although hint use improvedaccuracy most clearly at smaller orientation differences. In Experiment 2, mice sought information more often at lower grating coarseness, and hint use was associated with the greatestaccuracy benefit under those more difficult conditions. However, the critical test results did not support the prediction that information seeking would track the need for additional information.Mice frequently sought information in target-only trials, in which no additional information was required, and showed relatively low rates of information seeking in trials in which theinitial display consisted of two identical, and therefore nondiagnostic, stimuli. These findings indicate that information seeking in the present task was multiply determined. The observedpattern was consistent with contributions from competition, reinforcement history, and the behavioral utility of the hint. Although some aspects of training remained compatible withconfidence-based control, the critical test conditions showed that information seeking was not governed by confidence monitoring alone.

papers.title: Eliciting Spontaneous Belief-Congruent Action Anticipation in Adults Using Structured Familiarization in Rich Nonverbal Narratives
papers.authors: Fumihiro Kano, Josep Call, Nicolas Goppold et al.
papers.summary: Anticipatory-looking false-belief tasks are meant to show non-verbally that people predict actions from others' beliefs, but their reliability is debated. Across six experiments with 302 adults, the researchers kept the false-belief events fixed and reworked the familiarization phase within rich nonverbal narratives. Reliable belief-congruent looking appeared once familiarization was restructured, perhaps because that reduced reliance on spatial heuristics, and it replicated in a second lab. The takeaway is that these results depend heavily on the predictive structure of the procedure.
papers.abstract: Humans and other animals predict others’ actions from mental states, even when those states misrepresent reality. The anticipatory-looking false-belief (ALFB) task assesses belief-congruent action prediction without verbal responses, yet its reliability remains debated. Across six experiments, we tested 302 adults using false-belief events embedded in rich nonverbal narratives. We progressively refined familiarization while keeping the critical false-belief induction and test events unchanged. Reliable belief-congruent anticipatory looking emerged after familiarization was restructured, possibly because this reduced reliance on spatial heuristics and encouraged perspective taking. Explicit verbal prediction questions strengthened performance but were unnecessary. The refined procedure was confirmed within the original laboratory and independently replicated in a second laboratory. These findings indicate that belief-congruent action prediction is sensitive to task procedures, especially the predictive structure of familiarization. Our study provides a foundation for evaluating spontaneous theory of mind across development and species.

papers.title: On bias in detecting bias: A signal detection analysis of attributions to gender discrimination.
papers.authors: Marie Jakob, Anat Shechter, Jimmy Calanchini et al.
papers.summary: Across five studies on gender discrimination in corporate pay raises, researchers used signal detection theory to separate observers' sensitivity (spotting discrimination) from response bias (a tendency to say it's present). Prototypes of discrimination, and how well they matched the actual decisions, shifted response bias. The amount of harm done had a small effect on sensitivity and a large one on response bias, tied to people's sense of what a fair standard is. The work moves signal detection ideas about attributing discrimination from conceptual speculation to empirical tests.
papers.abstract: Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of signal detection theory, with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers' ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers' judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical signal detection theory analyses of attributions to discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1-3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2-4) inform observers' response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1-3), which reflects observers' determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing. papers.title: Spatial–numerical associations survive spatial frequency equalization in an adult unimanual SNARC task
papers.authors: Andrea Adriano, Michaël Vande Velde
papers.summary: One recent hypothesis says that non-symbolic spatial-numerical associations might just come from hemispheric differences in spatial frequency processing. To test this, adults compared dot arrays to a central reference with spatial frequency content controlled and with a single central response key, removing bimanual response confounds. Smaller numerosities were still processed better in left space and larger ones in right space, in both accuracy and reaction times. This weakens the spatial frequency account, at least in adults, and supports a genuine mapping of number onto space.
papers.abstract: The origins of spatial-numerical associations (SNAs), such as the SNARC (Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes) effect, remain debated. The Brain's Asymmetric Frequency Tuning (BAFT) hypothesis recently proposed that non-symbolic SNAs may arise from hemispheric asymmetries in spatial frequency (SF) processing, rather than reflecting a genuine spatial representation of number. Here we examined whether SNAs persist even in adult human cognition when both SF cues and, crucially, bimanual response confounds are eliminated. Participants performed a Go/No-Go non-symbolic magnitude comparison task, in which lateralized dot-arrays were compared to a central reference. Critically, all stimuli were controlled for low-level visual properties, including luminance and the SF power spectrum, thereby neutralizing potential SF hemispheric asymmetries. In addition, responses were executed using a single central key, removing any contribution of bimanual spatial coding. Results revealed a robust ratio effect, consistent with Weberian numerosity processing. Crucially, a significant SNARC congruency effect emerged in both accuracy and reaction times: relatively smaller numerosities were processed more efficiently when presented in the left visual space, whereas larger numerosities showed a right visual space advantage. Converging evidence from continuous regression analyses further supported this spatial-numerical mapping, showing an asymmetrical advantage for smaller magnitudes in left visual space and larger magnitudes in right visual space. This pattern persisted despite lacking SF asymmetries and bimanual response mappings. Together, these findings weaken the BAFT hypothesis, but only in adulthood, by showing that non-symbolic SNAs cannot be reduced to low-level visual or response-related confounds. Instead, they support a higher-order representation of numerical magnitude likely mapped onto space.
